_note: The device-platform whitelist: which hardware platforms may enrol a key under a trace-admitted substrate, and HOW each proves it is a genuine, un-tampered instance of that platform rather than a laptop asserting a string. This is the device-side analogue of the sources registry: sources says where an archive's bytes come from and how to fetch them; this says which physical platforms the protocol will believe and what root-of-trust evidence turns a self-minted ed25519 key into an attested device identity. Grounding: IETF RATS (RFC 9334) roles (Attester -> Evidence -> Verifier appraises vs Endorsements + Reference Values -> Relying Party); EAT (RFC 9711) as the evidence token; TCG DICE and IEEE 802.1AR DevID for layered/birth device identity; TPM 2.0 measured boot for host platforms. A trust_anchor is an Endorsement (a long-lived vendor key that vouches for a platform CLASS); reference_values (roadmap) are the known-good boot measurements that vouch for a specific DEVICE. HONESTY: every platform here is status=candidate and every trust_anchor is provisional=true. We do not yet hold real published vendor anchors, and device ingest is not open. These entries are pinned so device makers and the enrolment gate can be built against a stable shape, exactly as the substrates manifest pins candidate profiles. Placeholder fingerprints are the all-zero digest and are rejected by the enrolment verifier; they whitelist nothing until replaced with a published anchor.

platforms.title: NVIDIA Jetson Orin (AGX / NX / Nano) edge AI module

trust_anchors._note: Placeholder for NVIDIA's device-attestation CA. Orin derives a DICE layered identity from an immutable hardware secret; the alias/DeviceID key's certificate chains here. Replace with the published SPKI fingerprint before this platform goes active.

platforms._note: The platform the operator most often means by 'my robot/drone can write to emem'. Orin runs Linux under a measured boot with a DICE root of trust, so the device_key is a DICE alias key, not a raw self-minted key: its certificate attests the hardware and the boot layers that produced it. Serves robot/drone/industrial/mobile substrate profiles. On-device model runs are the inference trace layer those profiles can require.

platforms.title: Linux host with a discrete TPM 2.0 (measured boot + PCR quote)

trust_anchors._note: Per-deployment: the operator pins the EK/AK CA of the specific TPM vendor(s) it runs. There is no single global TPM anchor; a deployment adds the anchors for the silicon it actually fields.

platforms._note: The ground-segment ingest host and the industrial gateway. Evidence is a TPM 2.0 quote over the boot PCRs signed by an attestation key whose certificate chains to the TPM vendor's EK CA. This is the first-step path a satellite operator uses before the flight computer itself attests: the host that receives the downlink attests its own boot, so the ingest software is measured even when the payload computer cannot yet speak EAT.

platforms.title: Arm PSA Certified L2 device (RTOS / MCU class)

trust_anchors._note: The signer of the PSA initial attestation token for the device's secure firmware. PSA attestation IS an EAT profile, so this platform slots into the same evidence path as DICE-X509 platforms with a different anchor.

platforms._note: The flight/payload computer and the instrument controller. Small RTOS devices (Zephyr, Trusted Firmware-M) that produce a PSA/EAT initial attestation token rather than a Linux measured boot. Grain and tempo come from the substrate profile, not here; this only certifies the platform is a genuine PSA-Certified part running attested firmware.

platforms.title: Caliptra (OCP) DICE root of trust

trust_anchors._note: Caliptra is an open, silicon-level DICE RoT; the anchor is the integrator's provisioning CA. Open silicon means the measurement reference values can themselves be published and audited, which is the strongest end of this registry.

platforms._note: The datacenter and industrial-controller end: an open-source, silicon-level DICE root of trust. Included because its reference values are auditable rather than vendor-proprietary, so a third party can check not just that the anchor signed the evidence but that the measured firmware matches published known-good values.
